title: {{NAME}} and the Prehistoric Premier League
moral: Every problem looks impossible until someone decides to solve it anyway.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a young boy with brown hair and blue eyes, wearing a royal crimson soccer jersey with a gold crown emblem, black shorts, and crimson-gold cleats — same child, same face, same exact outfit in every image.

pages.content:
Princess Cora had a Stegosaurus.

This was unusual. Most palaces had horses or dogs or ceremonial birds.

Her Stegosaurus was named Dome and had arrived during a temporal event three years ago and had, subsequently, declined to leave.

Dome's hobby was football.

More specifically: heading the ball with its extraordinary dome-shaped skull, which sent the ball to approximately any location it intended with perfect accuracy.

Princess Cora had just entered Dome in the Royal Junior Football Tournament as her team's striker.

Everyone had concerns. {{NAME}} had a plan.

pages.content:
The concerns were legitimate: Dome was four times the size of any other player, its heading precision was extraordinary, and the rules said nothing about dinosaur strikers because nobody had needed to think about it before.

{{NAME}}'s plan: position Dome as a set-piece specialist only, bringing it on specifically for corners and free kicks, where its heading precision was most valuable and its size was least disruptive.

"The rest of the team plays normally," he told Princess Cora. "Dome comes on for specific situations."

"Can Dome understand specific situations?"

He looked at Dome, who was studying him with evident intelligence.

"Yes," he said.

pages.content:
The tournament: three matches, six set-piece situations where Dome came on.

Dome headed six balls. Four were goals. One was a cross that led immediately to a goal. One hit the crossbar from thirty metres, which was honestly impressive.

The rest of the team, freed from worrying about set pieces, played their best football.

Opposing teams had no precedent for marking a Stegosaurus at corners and generally made it up as they went, with limited success.

"This is technically unprecedented," the tournament director told {{NAME}}.

"It's in the rules," said {{NAME}}.

pages.content:
They reached the final.

The opposing team had, in the break before the match, figured out how to mark Dome: assign two of their biggest players to shadow it at all set pieces.

{{NAME}} anticipated this and modified the plan: Dome would draw the markers, {{NAME}} would take the corner to the far post instead.

It worked twice.

Final score: three-one.

Dome celebrated by headbutting the goalpost gently, which it had been told was not a foul in post-match celebrations, which was true.

pages.content:
Walking home in the evening, {{NAME}} thought about Dome sitting precisely in the position it was needed, waiting with expert patience for the correct tactical moment.

For a creature from a hundred million years ago, Dome had an extremely sophisticated understanding of modern football strategy.

"You're adaptable," he told Dome, who was walking beside him. "More than people think."

Dome made a sound like a bass drum.

He took it as agreement.

In bed that night, he fell asleep immediately, replaying the far-post corner that had won the final.
